I shall send troops after you as reinforcements.” Huang Zhong agreed and departed with Fa Zheng at the head of their own troops. Kongming told Xuande: “Unless that old general was provoked with words, he would accomplish nothing even if he went. Now that he has gone, however, we must dispatch troops to support him.” He therefore summoned Zhao Yun and ordered him to lead a force along a minor road as a surprise contingent in support: “If Huang Zhong is victorious, you need not engage; but if he suffers a reverse, go at once to his rescue.” He also sent Liu Feng and Meng Da with orders: “Lead three thousand men to strategic points in the mountains and set up many banners, thereby magnifying the apparent strength of our army and filling the enemy with alarm and uncertainty.” The three men each led their troops away. He also sent a messenger to Xiabian with a plan for Ma Chao, instructing him how to proceed. Then he sent Yan Yan to guard the passes at Langzhong in Baxi, relieving Zhang Fei and Wei Yan so that they might come and join the campaign for Hanzhong.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhang He and Xiahou Shang came before Xiahou Yuan and reported: “Tiandang Mountain has been lost, and Xiahou De and Han Hao have fallen. We now hear that Liu Bei is personally leading an army to seize Hanzhong. You should report swiftly to the King of Wei and ask him to send elite troops and valiant generals without delay to support us.” Xiahou Yuan immediately sent a messenger to inform Cao Hong. Cao Hong hastened through the night to Xuchang and reported the matter to Cao Cao. Greatly alarmed, Cao Cao urgently assembled his civil and military officers to discuss sending an army to save Hanzhong. Chief Clerk Liu Ye stepped forward and said: “If Hanzhong is lost, the Central Plain will be shaken. Your Majesty must not shrink from hardship, but personally lead the campaign.” Cao Cao said remorsefully: “How bitterly I regret not following your advice then, for it has brought us to this!” He hurriedly issued his command, raised an army of four hundred thousand, and set out in person. It was the seventh month of autumn in the twenty-third year of Jian’an. Cao Cao’s army advanced in three divisions: Xiahou Dun led the vanguard, Cao Cao himself commanded the center, and Cao Xiu brought up the rear. The three divisions set out one after another. Cao Cao rode a white horse with a golden saddle, wearing a jade belt and brocade robes. Warriors bore a great scarlet silk parasol adorned with gold. On either side were golden maces and silver axes, iron-shod staves, halberds, and spears. Banners emblazoned with the sun, moon, dragon, and phoenix flew aloft. Twenty-five thousand imperial guards, styled the Dragon and Tiger troops, formed five companies of five thousand, distinguished by the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black. Their banners, armor, and horses all matched the color of their company. The glittering spectacle was magnificent beyond measure.

p.src: After the army passed Tong Pass, Cao Cao, still on horseback, saw a dense and luxuriant grove. He asked an attendant, “What place is this?” The man replied, “It is called Lantian. Within that grove stands Cai Yong’s estate. His daughter Cai Yan now lives there with her husband, Dong Si.” As it happened, Cao Cao had been a close friend of Cai Yong. Cai Yong’s daughter Cai Yan had first been married to Wei Daojie; later she was carried off to the north, where she bore two sons and composed the “Eighteen Songs of a Nomad Flute,” which circulated throughout the Central Plain. Cao Cao took deep pity on her and sent men north with a thousand pieces of gold to ransom her. Fearing Cao Cao’s power, the Wise King of the Left sent Cai Yan back to the Han lands. Cao Cao then gave Cai Yan to Dong Si as his wife.

p.src: That day, when he reached the estate and recalled Cai Yong, Cao Cao ordered the army to continue ahead while he led more than a hundred mounted attendants to the gate and dismounted. Dong Si was then serving at a post away from home, so only Cai Yan was present. Hearing that Cao Cao had arrived, Cai Yan hurried out to welcome him. When Cao Cao entered the hall, Cai Yan completed the formal greetings and stood in attendance at his side. Cao Cao happened to notice a scroll depicting a stone inscription hanging on the wall. He rose to examine it and asked Cai Yan about it. Cai Yan replied: “That is the inscription on the stele of Cao E. In the time of Emperor He, there lived in Shangyu a shaman named Cao Xu, who could perform music and dance to entertain the gods. On the fifth day of the fifth month, he danced drunkenly in a boat, fell into the river, and drowned. His fourteen-year-old daughter wandered along the riverbank weeping for seven days and nights, then leapt into the waves. Five days later, she rose to the river’s surface bearing her father’s corpse on her back. The local people buried her beside the river. Du Shang, magistrate of Shangyu, reported the event to the court and memorialized her as a filial daughter. Du Shang ordered Handan Chun to compose an inscription and have it carved on a stele to commemorate the deed. Handan Chun was only thirteen at the time, yet he wrote the whole composition at a single stroke without making one correction. The stone was erected beside the tomb, and all who saw it marveled at him. My father Cai Yong heard of it and went to see it. By the time he arrived, night had fallen, so in the darkness he read the inscription by tracing the characters with his hand. Then he asked for a brush and wrote eight large characters on the back. When later generations recopied the inscription in stone, however, they did not carve those eight characters.” Cao Cao read the eight characters aloud: “Yellow silk, young wife; daughter’s son, mortar for spices.” Cao Cao asked Cai Yan, “Do you understand their meaning?” She replied, “Though they are words left by my late father, I truly do not understand them.” Cao Cao turned to his advisers and asked, “Do any of you understand it?” None could answer. Then one man among them stepped forward and said, “I have understood its meaning.” Cao Cao looked and saw that it was his registrar, Yang Xiu. Cao Cao said, “Say nothing yet; allow me to think it through.” He then took leave of Cai Yan and led his company out of the estate. After riding three li, he suddenly grasped the answer and said to Yang Xiu with a smile, “Now tell me your interpretation.” Yang Xiu said, “It is merely a word riddle. ‘Yellow silk’ is silk of a color. Place the silk radical beside the character for ‘color,’ and it forms the character ‘絕.’ A ‘young wife’ is a young woman. Place the character for ‘young’ beside the woman radical, and it forms ‘妙.’ A ‘daughter’s son’ is the child of a woman. Place ‘child’ beside the woman radical, and it forms ‘好.’ A ‘mortar for minced spices’ is a vessel for the five pungent herbs. Place ‘pungent’ beside ‘receive,’ and it forms ‘辭.’ Taken together, the four characters read ‘絕妙好辭’—‘an exquisitely fine composition.’” Cao Cao exclaimed in astonishment, “That accords exactly with my own conclusion!” Everyone marveled admiringly at the quickness of Yang Xiu’s wit and learning.

p.src: Within a few days, the army reached Nanzheng. Cao Hong came out to receive Cao Cao and gave him a full account of Zhang He’s affair. Cao Cao said, “The fault was not Zhang He’s. Victory and defeat are common fortunes of war.” Cao Hong said, “At present Liu Bei has sent Huang Zhong to attack Mount Dingjun. Knowing that Your Majesty’s army has arrived, Xiahou Yuan has held his defenses and not ventured out to fight.” Cao Cao said, “To refuse battle is to display cowardice.” He immediately sent a bearer of the imperial tally to Mount Dingjun, ordering Xiahou Yuan to advance. Liu Ye remonstrated, “Xiahou Yuan is too headstrong by nature. I fear he may fall into a treacherous scheme.” Cao Cao therefore wrote him a letter in his own hand. The envoy bore the tally to Xiahou Yuan’s camp and was admitted by him. The envoy produced the letter, and Xiahou Yuan opened and read it. It read in substance: “Every general must temper hardness with softness and must never rely on courage alone. He who depends only on valor is merely a match for a single man. I have now stationed the main army at Nanzheng and wish to see the display of your ‘wondrous talent.’ See that you bring no shame upon those two characters.”

p.src: Xiahou Yuan was delighted when he finished reading. After dismissing the envoy to return, he consulted Zhang He, saying, “The King of Wei now commands a great army at Nanzheng to campaign against Liu Bei. If you and I continue merely to hold this place, how can we ever achieve distinction? Tomorrow I shall give battle, and I mean to capture Huang Zhong alive.” Zhang He said, “Huang Zhong possesses both strategy and valor, and moreover has Fa Zheng to assist him. He must not be underestimated. The mountain roads here are steep and perilous; our only proper course is to hold fast.” Xiahou Yuan said, “If others win all the merit, with what face shall you and I appear before the King of Wei? You need only guard the mountain; I shall go out and fight.” He then issued an order: “Who dares go out on reconnaissance and lure the enemy forth?” Xiahou Shang said, “I am willing to go.” Xiahou Yuan said, “Go out on reconnaissance and engage Huang Zhong, but be sure to lose, not win. I have an excellent plan: do thus and thus.” Xiahou Shang accepted the command and led three thousand troops forward from the main camp at Mount Dingjun.

p.src: Now Huang Zhong and Fa Zheng had stationed their troops at the entrance to Mount Dingjun. Though they repeatedly issued challenges, Xiahou Yuan held firm and would not come out; they wished to attack, but feared the perilous mountain roads and could not judge the enemy's dispositions, so they had no choice but to hold their ground. One day, a sudden report came that Cao's troops were descending from the mountain to offer battle. Just as Huang Zhong was about to lead his men out to meet them, his subordinate officer Chen Shi said, “General, do not move. Allow me to face them.” Huang Zhong was delighted and ordered Chen Shi to lead one thousand men beyond the mountain entrance and form ranks. When Xiahou Shang's troops arrived, the two sides engaged. After only a few bouts, Xiahou Shang feigned defeat and fled. Chen Shi pursued him, but halfway onward, rolling stones and stone projectiles came crashing down from both mountains, preventing his advance. As he was about to turn back, Xiahou Yuan suddenly led troops out behind him. Unable to withstand them, Chen Shi was captured alive and taken back to their camp. Many of his soldiers surrendered. Some survivors escaped with their lives and returned to tell Huang Zhong that Chen Shi had been captured. Alarmed, Huang Zhong consulted Fa Zheng. Fa Zheng said, “Xiahou Yuan is impetuous by nature, relying on courage while lacking strategy. We should rouse the soldiers, break camp and advance, fortifying each step as we go, and lure Xiahou Yuan into battle so that we may capture him. This is the method of ‘turning from guest into host.’”

p.src: Huang Zhong adopted his plan and distributed all available goods among the army as rewards. Cheers filled the valley, and the soldiers vowed to fight to the death. That very day Huang Zhong broke camp and advanced, establishing a fortified camp at every stage; he remained in each camp for several days before advancing again. Xiahou Yuan learned of this. He wished to go out and fight. Zhang He said, “This is the stratagem of ‘turning from guest into host.’ You must not give battle; if you do, you will suffer defeat.” Xiahou Yuan would not listen. He ordered Xiahou Shang to lead several thousand men into battle, advancing straight to Huang Zhong's camp. Huang Zhong mounted his horse, took up his saber, and rode out to meet him. The moment he crossed weapons with Xiahou Shang, he captured him alive and returned to camp. All the others fled in defeat and returned to report to Xiahou Yuan. Xiahou Yuan hurriedly sent a messenger to Huang Zhong's camp, offering to exchange Chen Shi for Xiahou Shang. Huang Zhong agreed that they would make the exchange before the battle lines the next day.

p.src: The next day, both armies reached a broad place in the valley and drew up their formations. Huang Zhong and Xiahou Yuan each sat their horse beneath the gate banner of their own formation. Huang Zhong brought Xiahou Shang, while Xiahou Yuan brought Chen Shi. Neither prisoner was given robe or armor, but wore only thin garments covering the body. At the beat of a drum, Chen Shi and Xiahou Shang each ran back toward his own lines. Just as Xiahou Shang was reaching his camp gate, an arrow from Huang Zhong struck him squarely in the back. Xiahou Shang returned with the arrow still lodged in him. Xiahou Yuan flew into a rage, spurred his horse, and charged straight at Huang Zhong. This was precisely the fight Huang Zhong had sought to provoke. The two generals crossed horses and fought for more than twenty bouts, when the gong suddenly sounded in Cao's camp to recall the troops. Xiahou Yuan hastily wheeled his horse and returned, while Huang Zhong seized the advantage and attacked for a spell. Back in his formation, Xiahou Yuan asked the officer guarding the lines, “Why did you sound the gong?” The officer replied, “I saw banners of Shu troops at several places in a hollow among the hills. Fearing an ambush, I urgently recalled you, General.” Xiahou Yuan believed him and thereafter held firm without coming out.

p.src: Huang Zhong pursued as far as the foot of Mount Dingjun and consulted with Fa Zheng. Pointing with his hand, Fa Zheng said, “West of Mount Dingjun stands a lofty mountain, surrounded on every side by perilous paths. From that mountain one can look down and discern the true state of Mount Dingjun. If you can take it, General, Mount Dingjun will be as good as in the palm of your hand.” Huang Zhong looked up and saw that the summit was fairly level, with only a few men and horses upon it. That night, at the second watch, Huang Zhong led his troops forward with gongs ringing and drums beating, and charged straight to the summit. The mountain was guarded by Xiahou Yuan's subordinate Du Xi, who had only a few hundred men. Seeing Huang Zhong's great force swarm upward, they had no choice but to abandon the mountain and flee. Huang Zhong gained the summit, which stood directly opposite Mount Dingjun. Fa Zheng said, “General, you may hold the middle slope while I remain on the summit. When Xiahou Yuan's troops arrive, I shall raise a white flag as the signal, but you must hold your troops and make no move; once they are weary and off guard, I shall raise a red flag, and then you must charge down the mountain against them. By awaiting the weary in full strength, we are certain to win.” Huang Zhong was delighted and followed his plan.

p.src: Meanwhile, Du Xi led his troops back in flight and told Xiahou Yuan that Huang Zhong had seized the mountain opposite. Xiahou Yuan said furiously, “Now that Huang Zhong has occupied the mountain opposite, I cannot but go out and fight.” Zhang He remonstrated, “This is Fa Zheng's scheme. You must not give battle, General; you should only hold firm.” Xiahou Yuan said, “They have occupied the mountain opposite me and can observe my true condition. How can I not fight?” Though Zhang He pleaded bitterly, he would not listen. Xiahou Yuan divided his forces to surround the opposite mountain, hurling abuse and issuing challenges. On the mountain, Fa Zheng raised the white flag; no matter how Xiahou Yuan reviled him, Huang Zhong refused to come out and fight. After noon, Fa Zheng saw that Cao's troops had grown weary, their ardor spent, and that many had dismounted to sit and rest; he then unfurled the red flag. Drums and horns sounded together, and thunderous battle cries arose. Huang Zhong charged at the very front and galloped down the mountain with the force of heaven collapsing and earth splitting apart. When the sun rose in the east, they saw provisions piled as high as mountains. Only a few soldiers stood guard. At the sight of the Shu troops, they abandoned everything and fled. Huang Zhong ordered all his cavalrymen to dismount and pile firewood atop the grain. They were just about to set it alight when Zhang He’s troops arrived and became locked in a confused battle with Huang Zhong. When Cao Cao heard of it, he urgently ordered Xu Huang to go to the rescue. Xu Huang advanced with his troops and trapped Huang Zhong in the midst of the encirclement. Then more of Cao Cao’s troops arrived from behind and surrounded Zhang Zhu.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhao Yun waited in camp until noon drew near. When Huang Zhong still had not returned, he hastily donned his armor, mounted his horse, and led three thousand men forward to reinforce him. Before departing, he said to Zhang Yi, “Hold the camp firmly. Station plenty of archers and crossbowmen on both flanks as a precaution.” Zhang Yi repeatedly assented. Zhao Yun leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and charged straight ahead. A general barred his path. It was Murong Lie, an officer under Wen Ping, who urged his horse forward and flourished his saber to meet Zhao Yun. With a single thrust, Zhao Yun struck him dead. Cao Cao’s troops fled in defeat. Zhao Yun fought straight into the layered encirclement, where another body of troops blocked him. At their head was the Wei general Jiao Bing. Zhao Yun shouted, “Where are the Shu troops?” Jiao Bing replied, “They have all been slain!” Enraged, Zhao Yun spurred his horse forward and killed Jiao Bing with a single thrust. Scattering the remaining troops, he pressed straight on to the foot of North Mountain. There he saw Zhang He and Xu Huang surrounding Huang Zhong, whose soldiers had long been trapped. With a mighty shout, Zhao Yun leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and charged into the dense encirclement. He dashed left and broke through right as though entering a land devoid of men. His spear darted all around him like pear blossoms dancing in the air. It whirled about his whole body like auspicious snowflakes drifting down. Wherever he went, those who saw the banner bearing the four characters “Zhao Yun of Changshan” and knew of his valor at Changban in Dangyang passed the word among themselves and fled in every direction. Zhao Yun rescued Zhang Zhu as well.
